newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Central bank hints at Taiwan dollar depreciation.
newsitem.headline: Central bank hints at Taiwan dollar depreciation.

text.p: Taiwan central bank vice governor Liang Cheng-chin said on Tuesday the Taiwan dollar "in theory" should reflect the U.S. dollar's prolonged overseas rise, hinting that the bank would not oppose a depreciation.
"The Taiwan dollar in theory should reflect the U.S. dollar's strength overseas," Liang said in comments to reporters after the foreign exchange market closed for Tuesday.

Liang attributed the Taiwan dollar's persistent strength despite the U.S. dollar's sharp appreciation against the yen and other major currencies to "seasonal factors" -- a reference to strong demand for cash before the Chinese lunar new year.

He attributed Tuesday's Taiwan dollar rise to a big influx of foreign funds for China Steel Corp's overseas issue of global depositary receipts, part of the Taiwan government's privatisation of the formerly state-owned steelmaker.

Analysts said Liang's comments implied that the central bank would not oppose a depreciation of the Taiwan dollar after five-day new year holiday break, something that local dealers have said is all but certain due to the U.S. dollar strength.
Foreign exchange trading will stop on Thursday and resume on Tuesday, February 11.

The local dollar closed on Tuesday at T$27.438, back from an intra-session high of T$27.425 but nonetheless firmer than Monday's T$27.442 finish -- and well above the T$27.5 level at which it idled through the latter half of 1996.
Turnover through dealers on Tuesday was an active US$302.5 million, pushed higher by inflows of foreign funds in part to take up the state's offer of equity in China Steel.

The Taiwan dollar has effectively defied the U.S. dollar's dramatic rise against the yen, staying in lockstep with the greenback and even appreciating during the annual pre-holiday peak demand period in January and early February.
Dealers have cautioned that such a rise was unsustainable, saying the Taiwan dollar's strength threatened to undermine Taiwan's exports to Japan and other non-U.S. economies.

The central bank has said repeatedly that it was content to leave the Taiwan dollar alone, arguing that it should be allowed to find its own value through market forces and pledging not to intervene in the foreign exchange market.
Dealers have said there has been little sign of intervention by the central bank in recent months.
